title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
summary:
The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.
Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.
The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.
The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.

title: House Dems to introduce immigration bill establishing a 10-year expiration on final orders of removal
summary:
House Democrats will introduce legislation on Thursday that would provide relief to some immigrants who have final orders of removal but no criminal record, and create a pathway for them to obtain legal permanent residency.
A final order of removal is issued by an immigration judge or immigration authorities and requires a noncitizen to leave the country or be deported.
As of now, there is no expiration on final orders of removal.
Courtesy Kaur FamilyThe legislation would also create a pathway to lawful permanent residency for individuals with expired orders of removal.
The Department of Homeland Security and ICE have expanded enforcement in Trump's second administration against individuals with final orders of removal, including through deportations to third countries.

title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
summary:
We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content.
In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers.
The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA.
Second, trusted flaggers notify platforms of suspected illegal content—platforms must prioritize these notices and they have sole responsibility to decide to remove content.
Combining these powers blur enforcement and flagging functions, which the Commission’s own draft guidelines on trusted flaggers explicitly caution against.
